1311395,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.1.7.2,1943-06-09,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,,Minister of Labour,QUESTIONS,CONFERENCE ON INDUSTRIAL RECREATION,,1.
column2: Yes.
Recommendations:

Purpose: The purpose of a plan for recreation should be the provision of a programme of intrinsic worth to the individual, as well as to provide greater assurance of maintaining interest in production work on the part of the worker.

Pattern of organization: National advisory committee, provincial advisory committees, regional and local committees. Properly qualified paid personnel appointed to undertake the work of promoting recreational plans on national, provincial, regional and local levels.
Finances: There should be a four-way financial participation-workers, management, recreation councils or organizations, federal and provincial governments.
Personnel: There should be provision made for training personnel, if the need arises.
Facilities: Basic facilities already established in communities should be made available wherever required. Existing facilities should be fully used.

Programme: The programme should be sufficiently flexible and diversified to meet the needs of the workers and their families. Industry should be urged to develop recreational programmes within the plant when such programmes are advantageous.
Recreational programmes should be a community development within the areas where the establishment of war industries has created an urgent need.

An order in council, P.C. 4703, dated June 8, 1943, has been passed under authority of the War Measures Act authorizing the Minister of Labour to enter into agreement with provinces or municipalities to provide recreational facilities for war workers, and for an equitable sharing of costs by the dominion.

1311404,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.1.10.2,1943-06-09,58a4a9e8-42c9-4fe6-b9ae-c18e764d9a45,ca.m.2972,Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence,QUESTIONS,STORAGE OF GOODS IN OGDEN POINT, B.C., PIER WAREHOUSE",,"The questions arise out of a news item in the Globe and Mail which was read in the house by the hon. member for Peterborough West on Friday last.

In July, 1942, the Canadian Red Cross was offered cargo space for a large shipment of relief supplies to the far east. The vessel which was chartered by the American Red Cross Society was expected to sail in a few days.

Because of the large quantities to be shipped and the limited time, the Canadian Red Cross was not able to handle the shipment alone and most of the Canadian supplies were furnished by the Department of National Defence to the Canadian Red Cross for forwarding.

By the most strenuous efforts the supplies were procured, shipped to San Francisco and loaded on to the vessel only to find that the United States government could not get a safe conduct for her from the Japanese government. The supplies had, therefore, to be unloaded. The part of the shipment owned
by national defence was shipped to Victoria, placed in storage at Ogden pier and held intact in storage until the middle of January, 1943.

When it became evident that no means of transport under safe conduct was in sight, the part of the supplies that consisted of perishable foodstuffs was at once turned over to all arms of the service in the Pacific command for issue in the usual way. The balance of the foodstuffs was subsequently absorbed in the same way. Nothing was lost.

The only portions of the national defence supplies still held in storage at Ogden pier are clothing and a small quantity of medical supplies and these will be returned to stock and used by the armed forces.

1311411,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.2.1.2,1943-06-09,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY-TELETYPE MESSAGES IN FRENCH,SOURIS RIVER-USE OF WATER FROM RESERVE STORAGE DAMS,,On January 15, 1940, the governments of Canada and the United States referred to the International Joint Commission the question of the distribution of water of the Souris river as between the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba
Questions as Orders for Returns

and the state of North Dakota. This reference was made under article 9 of the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909. In the summer of 1940 representations were heard from all interested parties and on October 2, 1940, the commission handed down interim recommendations as to the use of the water. The interim recommendations were accepted by the government of Canada and the government of the United States and were approved by the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The recommendations provided for the release to Manitoba of a minimum quantity of water per year which amount was increased by a subsequent order of the commission dated November 17, 1942.

At present, the International Joint Commission has under consideration further representations made with respect to the equitable distribution of the water. Hearings were held in Minot, North Dakota, and Melita, Manitoba, on May 24 and May 26 respectively, at which all parties with an interest in the matter were given an opportunity to present their views. It is expected that a further interim recommendation will be made by the commission shortly. A permanent decision as to the distribution of the water will only be made after experience under interim orders has given further information and knowledge on which to base a satisfactory division.

1311435,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.9.1.2,1943-06-09,795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1,ca.m.1278,Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,ARGENTINE REPUBLIC,QUESTION AS TO RECOGNITION OF THE NEW GOVERNMENT,,Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct two questions to the Prime Minister arising out of reports respecting changes of government in the Argentine. What steps are in contemplation by this government towards a recognition of the new government of the Argentine? Has the Prime Minister received from the Canadian legation at Buenos Aires or the charge d'affaires of the Argentine legation in Ottawa sufficiently comprehensive reports upon which he could form a judgment as to how these events in the Argentine will affect the attitude of that republic towards Canada and the united nations generally?

,National Government,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1311436,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.9.1.3,1943-06-09,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,ARGENTINE REPUBLIC,QUESTION AS TO RECOGNITION OF THE NEW GOVERNMENT,,Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might reply to the second question first, as that will answer in part the first question. I
fMr. Mackenzie King.]

may inform the leader of the opposition that we have received extensive reports from our legation in Buenos Aires but that the political situation in that city will have to be very much clearer than it is at present before it would be safe to venture a firm prophecy as to the future. The only official statement so far issued by the new Argentine government indicates an intention to continue, for the time being at least, a policy of neutrality in relation to the war against the axis.

I do not think the change of government in the Argentine indicates any change of friendly feeling on the part either of the Argentine, its people and government towards Canada, its people and government, and in the circumstances the position of the Argentine continues as it has in the past.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL

HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour):,Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,WINNIPEG TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL- FREEZING OF WAGES OF LOW-PAID WORKERS,,Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 7, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked me if I had been advised of a complaint of the Winnipeg and district trades and labour council that the selective service officer in Winnipeg was freezing workers to low-paid jobs when other men were not available for the employers concerned. I had the director of employment service and unemployment insurance of my department telegraph to our regional employment officer at Winnipeg for a report. The reply which came yesterday is to the effect that no official complaint has been received from the trades and labour council. There had been a complaint made to that council by the business agent of the moulders union concerning a labour dispute between moulders and the Vulcan Iron Works of Winnipeg because of a decision on wages given by the Winnipeg regional war labour board. Forty moulders had requested the Winnipeg selective service office to grant permits for other jobs, but as the Vulcan Iron Works is designated an essential industry the
Man-Power
request was refused. The advice from Winnipeg is that the men are back at work in this plant pending an appeal of their case to the national war labour board.

,Liberal,,Humphrey Mitchell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97&Language=E&Section=ALL
1311443,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.10.1.3,1943-06-09,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. KNOWLES:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,WINNIPEG TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL- FREEZING OF WAGES OF LOW-PAID WORKERS,,May I ask the Minister of Labour if he has any information as to the nature of the other work that these men were seeking? My understanding was that they were seeking the same kind of work, in essential industry, at higher wages. The complaint was that they were being frozen in a low-paid job against a better paid job in an essential industry.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL
1311444,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.10.1.4,1943-06-09,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,Mr. MITCHELL:,Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,WINNIPEG TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL- FREEZING OF WAGES OF LOW-PAID WORKERS,,All I have is the advice I have received from the city of Winnipeg, and it is that the selective service officer told these men to return to their jobs in view of the priority' of that industry.

The situation has not changed. The federal government is doing everything it can do to provide in every community sufficient coal and to assist every community in obtaining sufficient fuel. Coal

we recognize as a federal problem. Fuel wood is a local problem in which the federal government is assisting to the utmost. We have certain operations for cutting quantities of fuel wood which can be moved into deficiency areas, but I think that that should not relieve any community of putting forth its own best exertions to meet its own fuel wood requirements.

1311471,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.16.1.1,1943-06-09,,,,stagedirection,,,,Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): As a member of this honourable house and as a French-speaking Canadian, I understand that at times translations of our debates and discussions are made in haste, but with regard to what was said on the occasion of the king's birthday the translation should have been polished ad unguem. Speaking on behalf of the young men of my constituency who are in the army, and being the last speaker on the subject, and speaking in French, on behalf of my fellow citizens whose maternal language is French, my last words on June 2 were as follow:
. . . j'offre nos respectueux hommages a sa digne epouse.
It was translated:
I present our humble respects to Her Majesty the Queen.

This is not at all what I said. It was ""I pay our respectful homage to his worthy consort."" As a member I feel very humble -I say that at times-but speaking as I did on behalf of the young men of the army and of the French-speaking citizens of Canada I was not feeling humble at all. But I was very respectful, and this is the shade of difference which should not be overlooked. I hope that in the future, as the translators do not come any more under you, sir, the Secretary of State will notify them accordingly.",,,,

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,LEGATIONS,PRESS REPORT AS TO REPRESENTATION OF SWEDEN IN CANADA,,Yesterday the leader of
the opposition drew my attention to a dispatch that had appeared in the Ottawa Journal of June 7, the significant part of which reads:
Increase of Sweden's consular and legation representation abroad, especially in Canada and South America, is contemplated in plans for the expansion of Sweden's foreign service.
My hon. friend then asked:

Will the Prime Minister inform the house whether or not negotiations have been entered into between the governments of Canada and Sweden along the lines indicated in the dispatch in question, and, if so, when such negotiations were commenced and how far they have progressed ?

I assume the Swedish government, like our own, is alive to the importance of developing, as opportunity permits, closer relations with other friendly countries and is making its plans for the necessary expansion in its diplomatic and consular services. Up to now, however, I have to inform the house, there have been no negotiations between the governments of Canada and Sweden looking toward the exchange of diplomatic representatives.

1311504,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.21.4,1943-06-09,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES,,,Thank you for the applause.
I may say that I am not surprised at the reaction of the present minister to some remarks I made. I have received nothing but

brickbats since I started in this game, because it is more or less a game, but a few more will not do me any harm. But, Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee the exact facts and the record. In the first place the minister was absolutely unfair yesterday. So far as his department is concerned, I made a bare statement of the case on behalf of the only people whom I try to represent when I endeavour to have a better deal for the men in our armed forces. The minister complained of my absence from the house. Well, for that matter I think it would be a good thing for me if I stayed away from the house altogether, because, as I have said before, parliament might just as well close up. We have been allowed to do nothing because our powers, functions and privileges have been taken away from us as a parliament and handed over to various control bodies. I have urged in the house that we should close about the end of the month. As a matter of fact, however, when the minister speaks of my absence, I was here on Monday night for a short time; but even when I was away I did not miss much anyway. I wish to thank you, Mr. Chairman, for your invariable kindness and courtesy to members of the opposition, because we look to you, and to your superior officer, Mr. Speaker, as referees to judge the play. I am a sportsman and not a politician; I have never been a politician. I have tried in this house to conduct myself like a gentleman and I have never on any occasion indulged in personalities. I have always tried not to forget the duty of ordinary Christian charity towards one's political opponents, and I have given the government a great deal of credit since the war started for what they have done when their efforts were for a total war. I may say further that at the time the minister spoke last night, unfortunately I was not here. I was out of the building for about half an hour. I was here from eight fifteen in the morning until twenty minutes before the minister started to speak, at which time I went out. While I was away he was referring to me, in my absence. At the time he spoke last night about absence there were only fourteen Liberals on the benches over there, and over here, right to the end of the overflow- only fourteen Liberals.

Yesterday afternoon the only minister on the government benches was my good and kind friend who has done so much in this war, both he and his family. I refer to the Minister of Agriculture. At the time he was the only minister in the house. Of all members of parliament, why am I singled out for attack? Why am I, of all members of the House of Commons, singled out by the
War Appropriation-Naval Services

minister for attack? It is because of one fact, namely, that I have supported in season and out of season rearmament and cooperation with Britain and our connection with the mother country, in peace, in war and all the time. I believe everything we have in this country by way of freedom, civilization and liberty we owe to the mother country. Our dominion was one of the chief drifters from the empire, between the two wars, and long before.

I may say that I referred to certain matters before the war started. I referred to what happened between 1938 and 1939, and after Munich. At that time I was bringing before the house consistently, when I was sitting in the seat now occupied by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the need for rearmament. On March 21, 1939, I called the attention of the Prime Minister, on a motion to go into ways and means, to the very grave danger this empire was in on land and sea and in the air, and the certainty of war. I said wfe had thrown away our defences, the finest army, air force and navy the world had ever seen. Then the huns entered Czechoslovakia. We had the Munich pact. And Munich was necessary because, as I say, France and Great Britain together, either singly or collectively, were no match for Hitler, were not ready for war, after throwing away their finest. Munich gave us a chance to get ready. As I said, on March 21, 1939, on a motion to go into ways and means, I called the attention of the house to this, that if the people were not told the facts, and if they were only told so much as their leaders let them know, then they were going to be led to disaster-which came in September.

On many other occasions I took the same stand. Return No. 140 was tabled-and I apologize to the committee for taking up this amount of time. However, it is not my fault. I was attacked, and I wish to place on record what the facts are. Facts are facts. As I said yesterday, I did not say and never have that I was a friend of the minister. I saw him only once, for a few minutes, at a football game in Toronto, I believe it was between Toronto in 1941-the Argonauts and Winnipeg. The last time I saw him, I believe, was about six o'clock last night, when I had a short conversation with him. That is the first time I had conversation with him about his department.

As I said, I received return No. 140 in 1939. In that I asked whether any steps had been taken by the government to secure a compulsory national register for Canada for defence or economic or industrial or labour

purposes. Secondly, if so, what were they, and thirdly, whether a census or modern doomsday book or national register will be ordered or compiled of (a) industrial power; (b) economic power; (c) food power; (d) manpower; (e) military and defence power, and (f) unemployed. I did not receive an answer to that return until a long time after. On every occasion I have said the same thing. If one reads the records of the house for May 26 and 28, 1938, he will find that I said:
At no time in the history of this empire has it been more necessary for the Dominion of Canada to give support, even if it is only moral support, to the motherland.

I called attention to our disarmament, that we had been wholly dependent on the mother country for our defence, on her navy, and that at no time had we been able to protect our own shores. I said at that time that I would have an opportunity to take it up with the Prime Minister later. He asked me to wait for the foreign affairs debate. He has known me a long time, and I have never had anything but great admiration for him and his family- because I have known him so long. I do not change. I have taken certain principles in the house, and I have stood by them. In that I have been consistent. I never have faltered once in changing my opinions with regard to the war, and the criminal mistake of disarmament, and what we owe to the mother country. In that connection the Prime Minister has taken a different stand. He is a gentleman who has extended a great deal of courtesy in the house. While I have not been of the same political faith, I have always found him courteous in debate toward opposition members, and always a gentleman.

There are just a few other matters I wish to refer to. I shall refer to the remarks last night of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, but will not read them. I shall give the page, and members who wish to do so may look it up. Last night the minister started off speaking about the Canadian navy and the navy league. I was connected with the navy league long before he was ever in politics. I was at that time chairman of the harbour board, had been on the school board, the police commission, and many organizations of that kind. We had the cadet movement in the school. The hon. member for Davenport had for many years taken a great deal of interest in the navy league. I believe he was in it before I was. And in that connection may I say that navy shows have been sent right across Canada at the expense of Canada with the Trade and Commerce department. The minister was kind enough to say that I should not expect kindness from him. I do
War Appropriation-Naval Services

not want kindness from him. I never said I was a friend of his. I have not known him long enough to be a friend of his. I said I was a friend of the mother country and of the navy, when he was supporting separatism and isolation, and all that kind of thing. I was standing for a better navy, and for protection. Where was he then? Where were the people lined up with him then? I may say that the minister talks about the navy league. It has done splendid work, I admit. I had a great deal to do with it in the city of Toronto, from which I come, both at the time of the last war and before.

The minister goes on to say that in 1926 the house was discussing the procedure to be followed in ratifying treaties. Mr. Chairman, the house was not discussing any such thing. The house was discussing a motion by Mr. Bourassa, who was then the hon. member for Labelle, to declare Canada a country independent altogether of the British empire. At that time I took a strong stand in the house.

I did not seek this fight, Mr. Chairman, but I am going to put the record right, because I have the right to do so, on this very question. Speaking in the house on June 21, 1926, in connection with Mr. Bourassa's motion in respect of foreign affairs, I said:

Of the links that used to bind Canada to the motherland, what links remain to-day? First, there is our allegiance to the British crown; secondly, there is the right of appeal to the privy council; thirdly, any treaties into which we enter must have the sanction of the mother of parliaments. . . . Sir John A. Macdonald was satisfied with the status of this country. He did not ask the British government to increase the status of Canada. Five hundred thousand soldiers who went to the front and fought for civilization in France and Flanders were satisfied writh Canada's status. Fifty thousand of those gallant men lie buried in those countries; they were content to fight even unto death under Canada's status. They fought for Canada's status, but did not ask that any change should be made in it; they did not ask for any increased status for Canada. Such being the case I think the civilians who stayed at home should also be satisfied with the status of this dominion.
I opposed that resolution, and that is what it was. I said:

The war did not change Canada's status. I am utterly opposed to any change in Canada's status. I am opposed to separatism autonomy, and further changing of our status. We are proud that Canada is an integral part of the greatest empire the world has ever known. The war left us our status as it was. What Canada has done the past thirty-five years she has done of her own volition and voluntarily and she would do the same thing over again, namely, come to the mother country's aid in her hour of peril. So the people of this country are satisfied with our present status.
Then in that speech I opposed the opening of the legation at Washington.

The minister made a further reference to 1926. Unfortunately I have not a staff of experts, as the minister has, to search the registry offices, to go to the newspaper offices and all that sort of thing. I can only write thirty letters a day, and as a member of the opposition I cannot get very much help, though I appreciate what has been done for me by the clerk and by you, Mr. Chairman. I have to do my own work, however, to dig up my own information, and to take part in these debates without any preparation. Yesterday in his remarks the minister referred to Collingwood, and I should like to say a word or two about the situation on the great lakes. Back in 1926 I referred to the situation which arose when a British ship was fired1 upon a number of times by a ship flying the United States flag, beyond the three-mile limit, and at that time I stated there were gun boats on the great lakes, contrary to the Rush-Bagot treaty. Then, at page 1335 of Hansard for February 25, 1926, when there were lake sailors drowned in the upper lakes in the November storms, I Went on to say:

It seems that we also in this country are content to sponge upon the hard earnings of the British taxpayers for the maintenance of our maritime freedom, and we forget the plight that this country would have found itself in during the late war if a German fleet had sailed up. the St. Lawrence or attacked Halifax or Saint John. In such an event what would have happened to Halifax, Saint John, Boston and New York? The British fleet to-day, Mr. Speaker, constitutes the real league of nations, while the league of nations is only a debating society and the results are of little or no value. So far as Canada's contribution to maritime freedom is concerned, we have two toy ships. Where are those ships? Off the Bay of Fundy? No; they are locked up in a garage in Halifax. Is that a self-respecting policy for the people of Canada to be proud of, a people who did so much in the late war, in the darkest hours of the empire, in giving of its best blood to the defence of our liberties? Are we prepared to depend altogether upon the British fleet without contributing to its upkeep? We have not spent a cent for the purpose. I doubt whether Mr. Mackenzie King was ever authorized by his cabinet to take the stand which he is reported to have taken in regard to the Locarno treaty. . . . We talk about our nationalism, but we are not a nation; we are part and parcel of the British empire. . . .
I went on to say that sooner or later Canada would have to live up to her responsibilities as a member of the British commonwealth, or declare herself independent of that commonwealth.

Then the minister went on to quote from page 4787 of Hansard for June 21, 1926. At that time we had no fleet; we did have a small navy, consisting of two or three ships, most of them obsolete and used only for
War Appropriation-Naval Services

purposes of good-will cruises and recreation. If they had put to sea from Halifax, what could they have done? As I said, if they saw an enemy ship coming along they could not fire their guns until they had cabled to Ottawa and an order in council had been passed. Otherwise they could not fire a pinwheel, a fire cracker or a sky rocket in defence of their country. Was that a self-respecting policy for the people of this country, the fifth trading nation of the world-to be completely dependent upon the mother country for the maritime freedom we then enjoyed? I say it was not, and1 I do not propose to have the stand I took on that or any other occasion misrepresented by anyone. I did not see the remarks of the minister until after twelve o'clock to-day and I have not had the necessary time to prepare a complete reply, but I should like to recall what I said in reference to a great disaster which occurred on the great lakes, and I quote from page 104 of Hansard for February 1, 1928:

The mother country produced a great Liberal between 1870 and 1880, Samuel Plimsoll, M.P., who directed his efforts against what was known as coffin ships, and who forced legislation to provide for seaworthy ships and life saving aids and help to navigation. . . .
The Conservative party in Great Britain wanted to postpone the introduction of the Plimsoll legislation, but Mr. Disraeli, ,the great persuader, insisted that it be carried through. Then I said:

There is no Plimsoll in the House of Commons here, and perhaps there is no public opinion to enable a man to do Plimsoll's work if he tried. There is no leader among the hon. gentlemen opposite who has as much true and genuine liberalism in his whole body as Benjamin Disraeli had in his little finger.
Then I went on to refer to the disaster on the great lakes:

The closing days and nights of navigation in the season of 1927 recorded a great story of unbroken fortitude and of unshaken endurance which proved that our countrymen, the sailors on the decks of those doomed vessels, were blood brothers of the soldiers who brought glory to Canada at St. Julien, the soldiers who could not be blown off the ground they gained at Passchendaele, who climbed the heights of Vimy Ridge, who gained the victory at Amiens and many another field of glory, men whose names will forever thrill every true Canadian. These sailors struggled or waited hour after hour; if help came to them it was help organized by the valiant hearts and strong bodies of their own country, or if help came it was help bought and paid for by the taxes of the people of the United States. That is Canadian nationality for you. The struggle was a story of glory for Canada's sailors. The struggle was a story of shame for Canada's politicians. The tragedies of the great lakes in the closing hours of navigation last season showed in its true colours the stuff that Canadian nationalism is made of.

. . . Canada is a proud and haughty nation. It sends its merchant ships into the winter storms with nothing to do but whistle for a United States service tug when the ship is in danger and to fill the air with the distress signals of a siren with the hope that a United States life saving vessel will put to sea and save the lives of Canadian sailors. Canada, a nation, and in trouble, has a navy maintained at the expense of the old country taxpayer to guard the safety of Canada's shores in war.

That is my reply to the minister. I admit my statements at that time, but the minister read only two or three sentences from an eight-page speech dealing with the whole history of Britain's aid to Canada; he read only a few words about the navy being locked up in a garage in Halifax. Well, it may have been just as well that they were locked up, because the ships were obsolete. If they put to sea in battle I doubt if anyone would be safe to go on them. Here is a return which the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) tabled giving the names of the fleet and the total tonnage on February 14, 1938. It was not as much in total as one tramp vessel of 10,000 tons. Two or three thousand tons, and these tramp steamers have tonnages as high as nine or ten thousand tons. That was the navy we had. That was our defence. The result was that we faced invasion and insult. I predicted that the enemy would come up the St. Lawrence.

He has had wide experience as a deep sea yachtman.

I belong to a yacht club but I never had any deep sea experience. Our fleet at Halifax was not let out of the garage to go into the deep sea. When our ministers wanted to go to Europe for the league to abolish all navies they did not take the Canadian navy; they headed for New York and took the ss. George Washington and Queen Mary and other boats from there. The return continues:

column1: The government were not satisfied with this one instance; they brought a lot of people from Hollywood to film shows for our silent fleet and sent them on a trip across Canada to tell us all about the navy. The minister referred to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I never in my life criticized the Minister of National Defence. I was referring to what had taken place at Christie Street hospital when the government in 1926 fired a lot of overseas soldiers who had had considerable experience and replaced them with men who had been nominated by the Liberal ward association.

Then we pass on to 1940. At that time the hon. member for Victoria, BO. (Mr. Mayhew), a most popular member, had been reported in the newspapers here as having stated that a naval college was to be located in Victoria. The minister was asked about this by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) and he replied that he had no information. I understood that negotiations had taken place for a site there and I suggested that it would be better to let parliament know something about it first.

The minister went on to quote another statement of mine as to the need of great Atlantic escorts, but I was really quoting a statement by Mr. Lyttelton, the British minister of production, which had been made in New York on November 11 last and in which he warned the dominion and the United States of the great danger in the Atlantic from submarines. I said:
We seem to have been trusting to Providence more than the Canadian navy.
The words I used were:
We seem to have been trusting to Providence as -well as to the Canadian navy.

I did not get the draft of my speech, but those were the words I used. I never cast any reflection upon the personnel of the department. If hon. members will read Hansard they will see that that is so, but what has been done is to take only one or two sentences of my remarks.

Then I brought up the question of holding civilian inquests. These soldiers are losing their civilian rights. I discussed this matter with the former attorney general of Ontario, Mr. Conant. It cost the province $65,000 to prosecute an airman for murdering a girl on Toronto island. We have 5,796 officers wearing uniform who before their appointment had never had any training. I was insisting that we should have a system, as in the last war, of civilian inquests in the three forces so that these men would not lose their civilian status.

I do not care a farthing what the minister says or thinks about me. I am not here for that purpose. There is something more noble than personalities to be considered. I have never attacked anyone personally since I have been in this house, and this is the first time I have been attacked. It was not until Monday night and last night when the minister made the statement he did. However, what I [DOT] said in the past twenty years is on the record. The record would not be complete without giving a list of the speeches I have made on different occasions, calling attention in 1937 to 1939 to our danger of invasion. On May 18 I referred to the laissez faire policy of the government and I called attention to the fact that there should be more navy cooperation with the other dominions and the mother country in the great crisis that faced us. I contended that the government was not doing its duty and were not letting the people know all the facts. I refer hon. members to Hansard of February 9, 1937, page 759, and also remind them that in April, 1938, I predicted the war. On July 1, 1939, I referred to the crisis that was developing and again predicted the war. I called attention to the inadequacy of our fleet and stated that Canada was asleep
War Appropriation-Naval Services

while her politicians dreamed and did nothing. I predicted that when war broke out we would be attacked. At page 794 of Hansard of 1926, on April 1, i939, on May 24, 1938, and again in 1939 you will find statements about our duty to our navy and to the men of the navy. You will see where I praised the personnel of our navy and regretted that they had to suffer as they had. Here is a return which gives certain figures about the navy. I wanted a naval college established, and a grant to the Singapore base and. to adopt the Jellicoe report, and I would train five or ten thousand cadets a year. The minister is quite proud that Britain has given us two destroyers, but we could have had these long before the war but we would not take them. We thought we were independent. We were depending on the Monroe doctrine, the League of Nations, the Locarno agreement, the Kellogg pact and all kinds of scraps of paper, for our defence on land and sea and in the air.

As I said last night, I have no quarrel at all with the minister, I have always looked upon the House of Commons as a gentleman's club, and have always treated everybody here with courtesy. I have never indulged in personalities. I have always obeyed the rulings of the Chair. I have said nothing inside or outside the, house that I would not say to a member himself publicly in the house. If I did not think something of my responsibility as a member of parliament I would have walked across the floor of the chamber last night and settled this thing with the minister. I think that is far the better way. If I am going to be attacked any more I want to know about it. You know what fair play is, Mr. Chairman. I have known for many years the minister who preceded the present Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I call him master of ceremonies. But the other night he hauled his rule book out of his pocket and quoted the rules quite unnecessarily on me. You know, Mr. Chairman, that a teferee does not want unseemly wrangles and to be forever hauling out his rule book and reading it to the players. The fact is that if we had more of the spirit of sportsmanship in this house we would get along far better and would not have such things as happened last night and this long debate on the war appropriation bill would have been ended long before now.

1311505,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.21.5,1943-06-09,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. GILLIS:,,NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES,,,Mr. Chairman, I suppose now it is permissible to say something about the navy. It is difficult to know just how to begin, because so far I have heard everything discussed except the navy estimates. I am sure that most members of the house are not interested in the debate that has been

carried on for the major part of this afternoon and last night. The people of Canada are fully aware that Canada was totally unprepared for war when war broke out and are not interested in any quarrels at this time across the floor of the house between the two major parties that held power from time to time in Canada. All such quarrels are irrelevant because both these parties must share responsibility jointly for our state of unpreparedness at the beginning of the war. I shall try, Mr. Chairman, to deal with the matters set out in the estimates. I want to bring to the minister's attention one or two things that come within his department and I do it not by way of criticism, but rather to focus his attention on them with a view to eliminating what I consider to be grievances.

But first let me say this. Personally I feel that our navy organization in Canada, starting from small things at the beginning of the war, is an organization distinctly Canadian. In the organization of our air force and our army we had the assistance to some extent of people from other parts of the world. But our navy started from nothing and it has been built up and has done a very creditable job as a purely Canadian organization. In addition, as the minister pointed out in his statement, the navy has in complete command on a war front the one and only Canadian who is in command in any theatre of war. That is to the credit of the navy. It indicates to me that in the administration of the navy regard is paid to the development of a Canadian force with Canadian responsibility and Canadian direction. I think that is as it should be, and I want to compliment those in charge of the navy-, and particularly the minister, on that trend. Personally I do nqt think that Canada, in view of the contribution she made in the last war and is making in this war, should be taking direction from any other part of the world. It is time we began to stand on our own feet. Perhaps the reason we were in the mess we were in when war broke out was that we had been sitting back and doing no probing for ourselves but were just accepting everything as gospel that was given to us from another part of the world. That is something I never agreed with and never will agree with. I think we should use our own eyes and our own ears, build our own economy and protect ourselves, instead of blindly accepting a lead from any other part of the world. The responsibility for the mess we found ourselves in when this war broke out was not in my opinion Canadian.
War Appropriation-Naval Services
Tt was because some people had been, sitting back and doing a lot of wishful thinking and accepting somebody else's advice.

I would like to bring the minister's attention to the necessity of granting free transportation to the members of the naval forces When they go home on leave. I lay stress particularly on the position of the sailor who comes home on leave after being at sea for six or eight months, as many of them are. Many of these boys come from the central west, from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and whether they land on the east coast or the west coast they have a considerable distance to travel to reach their homes when they get a couple of weeks leave, which they need and have earned. As it is now, they are Obliged to pay their own railway fare when going home across half this country on leave. I am sure that any member who has travelled to or from either coast will remember seeing many of these boys travelling second class, Sitting up in the coaches two or three nights on end, and travelling under very uncomfortable conditions in order to get home on leave. It is not too much to ask that after coming off the water where they have to sleep in their clothes for weeks and months at a time, these boys should be given free transportation to and from their homes. I would ask the minister to think that over. We have already suggested free transportation for the army and the air force on embarkation leave and on their regular furlough.

I emphasize that it is absolutely necessary because many of our sailors have to travel a considerable distance to reach their homes in the central west, in Saskatchewan and Alberta, for instance. I hope the' minister will give this request his sympathetic consideration.
, Last session when the minister had his estimates before the house I spoke of the merchant marine and the necessity of having ship masters keep a registration of their men

on board merchant ships in order that, if something happened to them, there would be some way of getting in touch with their next-of-kin and informing them of just what happened. During the past year I have received many letters from fathers and mothers on the east coast inquiring as to the whereabouts of a son who had left home perhaps a year or six months before and had gone aboard a certain ship. The ship is Norwegian, perhaps, or Greek, but is under British registry. The boy has been missing for some time. I write the shipping board in Montreal-that is, the British Ministry of Shipping. If the ship is of Norwegian registry one is obliged to get in touch with the Norwegian consul either in Saint John or Montreal; and my experience in writing these people on several occasions inquiring as to the whereabouts of a boy who had sailed on one of these ships is that I have never had an answer. As a result, some mother and some father go on month after month wondering as to the whereabouts of a missing boy. I know this matter comes under the Department of Transport, but I think it is time the naval authorities undertook the simple proceeding of issuing instructions to the shipping masters, where the boys ship out, or to the manning pools from which they are sent, tha-t a register of the address of next-of-kin of Canadian boys who are shipping on these boats of foreign registry should be kept, so that the parents could get in contact with the different centres when enough time has elapsed to indicate that something may have happened to the boy. Consideration might be given to that by the minister's department.

Another complaint which I have comes from nurses throughout Canada who desire to enter the naval service. I have corresponded with the minister on two or three occasions during the past thirteen months endeavouring to ascertain if it was possible for nurses who wished to enter the naval service to obtain appointments. The minister advised me that there was a long waiting list and that they were not being taken into the service very rapidly. But I believe the system is not handled on the basis of first come first served, because in the cases as to which I corresponded with the department, applications had been in for the past fourteen months. One of the girls I referred to had received a call, was given her medical examination, and was advised that she would be notified in due course. That puts her in a position where periodically she has to spend money to replace her uniform and make certain
War Appropriation-Naval Services

preparations if she is to stay in the hospital, though at the same time she is waiting a call to the navy. I am convinced that there is something to be desired in the consideration which is given to taking girls into the nursing service of the navy. If the merit system prevails, seniority of application and everything else being equal, that is the basis on which selections should be handled. I am reasonably sure that that is not the case at the present time. The girls to whom I make reference
column2: could have gone into other

column1: branches of the service but they did not want to, having a particular yen for the naval service. I suggest that the minister look into the situation with a view to establishing a system which is fair and equitable.
There is another matter upon which I wish he would make some observations, if not now, when he has had a chance to check up concerning it. On March 12, as reported in Hansard, page
column2: 2603, the Minister of

column1: Munitions and Supply, in discussing shipbuilding, was asked the following question by the hon. member for Vancouver South:
That would mean that we would have over two hundred ships less sinkings.
The minister replied:

Yes. Those ships are being chartered to the United Kingdom and will be reclaimed at the end of the war. We hope to have at that time sailors and officers from among the men presently in the Canadian navy. We expect that the Canadian merchant marine will be a substantial source of employment in the post-war years and that it will be of real benefit to Canadian post-war commerce. That is the policy.

What I am interested in is this. Canada is and will be for some time an exporting nation. In the past she had chartered ships from every part of the globe and paid out good Canadian money to have our produce taken to other parts of the world. I take it from the minister's statement that it is anticipated that full use will be made of our merchant marine in the aftermath of this war. That is as it should be. It will provide a means of livelihood for a large number of men who are now taking specialist training in that particular calling. As one who is interested in post-war employment I am in accord with that statement. What I would like the minister to' comment on is, how it is anticipated that the merchant marine will be built up, and how men now serving in the navy and in the merchant marine will be employed; the basis upon which this will be done. Will it operate by private enterprise as it is done now, with a certain amount of

governmental supervision? To what extent and in what capacity will officers and men now serving in the navy be utilized? Any information which the minister may have that will supplement the partial statement made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply would, I think, be welcome, because the statement we have already had_ requires some elaboration. It is something in which the Canadian people are definitely interested. We think it very necessary, instead of chartering ships from Japanese and all over the world to carry Canadian commerce to all parts of the globe, that it should be a definite phase of our own economic life after the war.

I am sorry I have had to occupy this amount of time and to deviate to some extent from the item we are considering, but after listening to the last speaker I thought I was justified in taking a little latitude and putting these particular questions to the minister to be answered after he has had time to study them.

1311512,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.21.12,1943-06-09,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. DIEFENBAKER:,,NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES,,,I have not as yet

taken any part in the discussion of this department under the war appropriation measure. May I begin by saying that all of us are proud of the navy and its activities, and those of us who come from western Canada, particularly far removed from the sea, are pleased that our provinces have made such a large contribution. Now that a new system has been evolved whereby ratings will be raised to commissioned rank, speaking on behalf of the western provinces our proportion of commissioned officers should be larger than it is now. An examination of the figures shown on page 3407 indicates an inequality in the percentages among the various provinces that is difficult to understand. In Prince Edward Island the proportion is 49 officers to 1,036 ratings, or one in 20; in Nova Scotia-one can understand this-one in 9; in New Brunswick, one in 13; in Quebec, one in 6%; Ontario, one in 12; and when you come to Saskatchewan the proportion is approximately one to 28; while in Manitoba it is about one in 20. Having regard to the quality of the men who are coming from the west I do think that there should be some equalization in the opportunities of commissioned rank and I have no doubt that will be so under the new arrangement.

Mention has been made of the fact that Canada's navy as a separate entity had its birth since the beginning of this war. In that connection I would point out that in 1918, on May 17, an agreement was made among the
War Appropriation-Naval Services
various dominions of the empire respecting naval development in the dominions. I will read it:

The dominion ministers, having considered the admiralty memorandum of May 17, 1918, on the naval defence of the British empire, which was circulated to the imperial war conference of 1918, submit the following conclusions and observations:

column2: The proposals set forth in the admiralty memorandum for a single navy at all times under a central naval authority are not practicable.

Purely from the standpoint of naval strategy, the reasons thus put forward for the establishment of a single navy for the empire under a central naval authority, are strong but not unanswerable. The experience gained in this war has shown that in time of war a dominion navy (e.g., that of Australia) can operate with the highest efficiency as part of a united navy under one direction and command established after the outbreak of war.

It is thoroughly recognized that the character of construction, armament and equipment, and the methods and principles of training, administration and organization, should proceed along the same lines in all navies of the empire. This policy has already been followed in those dominions which have established naval forces.

column1: 4- For this purpose the dominions will welcome visits from a highly qualified representa-t;je of the admiralty, who, by reason of his ability and experience, would be thoroughly competent to advise the naval authorities of the dominions in such matters.

5. As naval forces come to be developed upon a conisderable scale by the dominions, it may be necessary hereafter to consider the establishment for war purposes of some supreme naval authority upon which each of the dominions would be adequately represented.

In the very full statement that was given by the minister I do not find any reference to several of the matters covered by this memorandum of 1918, which to all intents and purposes has not since been altered. Are the principles of training, administration and organization alike, or have they proceeded along similar lines, in the various navies in the empire? Is there to-day a supreme naval authority within the empire upon which each of the dominions is represented? Is Canada represented on such a central board, and are any of the other navies within the empire represented on such a board?

_ The next matter I should like to deal with is one that has been referred to on previous occasions but it has yet to be answered by any of the ministers of defence. I intend to devote the time at my disposal to the consideration of a subject which is of interest not only to the men who serve in the navy but also to hose who serve in the other armed forces,
namely, the establishment, for the protection of service men and women, of a system of life insurance.

A number of questions were asked to-day by the member for Victoria-Carleton as to what insurance is offered to the members of the armed forces. Several other questions were asked at the same time, and the answer was, that insurance was made available by various insurance companies. I wish to place before the minister the necessity of action being taken now, before the commencement of the offensive overseas, for the establishment of a plan of life insurance which will be available to the men and women of the armed forces during the period of the war.

I realize that insurance can be secured from private companies, but the premiums are so high, having regard to the reasons incidental to war service, that it is impossible for service men and women to secure insurance to-day. It may be said that it is late in the war to suggest this, but I would point out that so far our casualties do not amount to over 8,000. It may also be argued that an insurance scheme will cost a great deal. It may cost the state a considerable outlay to protect the loved ones of those who are serving, who to-day, not being dependents, have no protection, but it would improve the morale of the armed forces in the knowledge that they would receive the same consideration and protection as given those in the United States armed services, and it would encourage thrift and give to those in the armed services a nest-egg after the war.

It has been most successful in the United States. Our armed forces serve alongside those from the United States, and I think that with a view to securing as nearly as possible an equality of terms of service, the introduction of this measure at this time would receive the approval not only of those in the armed forces but also of the people of Canada as a whole. The United States has had a national service life insurance scheme in effect since October 8, 1940. So successful has the scheme been that up to March 15, 1943, 7,750,000 applications had been received, with an average amount of $6,381 for each policy. It might be argued that to bring in such a scheme would impinge upon the field enjoyed by private insurance companies. However, experience in the United States of America is that fears such as that have not been justified in respect of the scheme introduced there. They had a similar scheme during the last war, altered in this war in order to meet the exigencies peculiar to present-day conditions.
In a recent article dealing with this matter the answer is given as to the effect on private insurance companies:

The advent of the government into the life insurance business during the first world war, authorizing and emphasizing as it did a maximum of $10,000 protection on every serviceman's life, has generally been conceded to have been a great benefit to the institution of privately operated life insurance. At that time apprehension was felt in some quarters of the possible encroachment of government upon the field of life insurance. As a matter of fact the records disclose that on January 1, 1917, there was less than twenty-five billion dollars of commercial life insurance in force in the entire United States, and within two years after the close of the first world war this amount had increased to over forty billion dollars, exclusive of government life insurance.

I suggest-and I am going to ask the [DOT]cooperation of the minister in this matter-the [DOT]establishment in Canada of a system of life insurance, made available, as I have already suggested, for every serviceman and woman, in amounts up to $10,000 per year, at net premium rates based on the Canadian table of mortality, with interest at three per cent, the government bearing the excess mortality costs.

As I have already stated, a similar system is in effect in the United States, and it has .worked out so successfully that wherever one goes among members of the service in that country, he hears good reports of the plan. I had an opportunity to speak to a number of servicemen on a recent trip to the United States, and they, along with those in public life, state that no scheme has ever been introduced in the United States which has done so much to improve the morale of those who serve.

I shall epitomize, in a very few words, the scheme in that country. It provides that insurance may be taken out by all who serve within 120 days after the scheme is brought into effect, or within that period after a person joins the armed forces. The premium is based on a five-year term insurance, with the privilege of conversion to ordinary life insurance, twenty-payment or thirty-payment, at any time within the period of five years. I shall not go into the scheme in detail, but I might say it is set out in the May issue of a publication called, ""The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science"".

Policies on maturity, on the death of those in the service, are payable to the beneficiaries, irrespective of pension rates enjoyed by those beneficiaries, by monthly payments, on the basis of $3.97, and up, per $1,000 of insurance. The cost is very low, having regard to the

I do not see why a line should be drawn as between those who enlisted before June 1, 1942, and those who joined after that date; certainly it is penalizing those who joined later. So far as the cost of living is concerned they are in exactly the same position as those who joined before June 1, 1942, and it seems to me there is a great deal of discrimination here. You ask these men, some of whom enlisted before June 1, 1942, and

others who enlisted later, to live under exactly the same conditions, to belong to the same force and fight for the same cause; yet one receives only $125 a day as against $1.45. A great deal has been said in eulogy of the boys of the navy. I would not want to detract in any way from what has been said in that regard, because I think the work they are performing is just as essential as the work of any other branch of our defence forces. I believe they are entitled to a little praise, but I think they are also entitled to a little financial consideration and in this respect I do not believe they are getting fair treatment. I am told that the reason why this change was made was to bring these rates into line with those of the other forces; the minister will correct me if I am wrong in that. Well, if that is true, it seems to me a very poor reward for the splendid service the navy is performing, to reduce the pay of the ratings by twenty cents a day. No doubt to some twenty cents a day may not seem very material, but when they were getting only $1.45 to start with and that has been reduced by twenty cents, it becomes a serious matter to these young fellows. Not only is it a consideration financially; it is a consideration in regard to their morale and feelings, and those are matters to which we should give attention.

Surely the excuse that this was done to bring them into line with the other services is hardly sound. It seems to me the fair thing in a case of that kind would be to increase the pay in the other services, instead of reducing the pay of these naval ratings, to bring them all somewhere near a decent standard. We cannot expect enlistments in the forces if we are not going to treat the men properly. Apparently the minister is having no difficulty in getting recruits; I think he said he has a waiting list, though not as large a list as he had previously. The air force also has a waiting list, though not as large a list as it had previously. The army is finding it difficult to get recruits; in fact we have had to resort to conscription for that purpose. This is a very poor way to encourage young fellows to join the navy. I suggest to the minister that this matter should be gone into a little more fully and that these men should be given their former pay and allowances when they are living out of barracks. If necessary, the allowances given in the other services should be increased as well. I need not say more on this matter until I have heard the minister's explanation. Those were the two subjects I wanted to bring to his attention.

1311583,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.23.67,1943-06-09,b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442,ca.m.5903,Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury):,,EDITION,,,I may not be correct in the designation of the plant which was built there, but an extensive operation was undertaken and is at that point. Also there are huge ammunition dumps in the locality, and one bomb from a submarine could explode the whole thing. Why was there so much concentration at that point? Point Edward, I understand, is on Sydney harbour. My information is that Sydney harbour proper is frozen for four months in the year; ships have to use the outside port in winter time. How can you have a naval base which is infested with ice? Not only is the harbour proper frozen over, according to the information I have, but the drift ice in the early part and the latter part of the season makes it more or less inaccessible. Is it intended to use ice-breakers to maintain this as an open port the year round?

Then I should like to have the minister's explanation as to the character of the construction there. My understanding is that the buildings were put upon filled land, that the concrete was poured and that on account of the instability of the foundation the backbone

of the building was broken and the work had to be done over again at great expense. It would appear from what I have heard that faulty judgment was used with respect to the construction at Point Edward. I should like to have the minister's defence on these two projects.

Then I wish to know why the minister has not gone ahead with the proposals for the arrangements at Saint John. Surely they are entitled to that, after all that has been said and done. It is a very moderate installation that was contemplated. The land was purchased, I believe, but no construction has taken place. I once told the minister that if he would come to Saint John, New Brunswick, we would bring out the bagpipes and give him a good, decent reception, but I am afraid that invitation will not hold out indefinitely unless he does something. I undertake that if he visits that city he will have a friendly greeting, because Saint John is intensely interested in the navy. There is no doubt that the people are navy-minded. They have had a volunteer naval reserve there for a long time, and I remember that, years ago, when I was connected with the navy league, no community was more ready to befriend it than the city of Saint John.

I think the minister owes an explanation of why New Brunswick has been, if I may use the expression, ignored. .The minister took great exception to an editorial in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal which the hon. member for St. John-Albert quoted at some length here the other evening, but I wish to tell the minister that that editorial exactly reflects the views of the people of that city, and he might as well know that from me.

I am not critical of the minister. I want to see the navy grow; I want to be considered a friend of the Canadian navy. I am very proud of our navy; I have a number of friends serving in it, and I hope it will be perpetuated after the war as one of the armed services of which Canadian citizens can be proud. I am sure it will be. I only wish we had more capital ships-I used inadvertently once before the expression ""fighting ships"" when I meant capital ships-in order that we could take a real part in the invasion of Europe, and so that it could be said to our glory that the Canadian navy had a part in what happened on the other side. It is not our fault; it is not the fault perhaps of anybody present, that
War Appropriation-Naval Services

we have not done more in this regard, but I have always felt that Canada was derelict in her duty towards the navy that protected our trade lines, our sea lines, our life lines; and during the period three years ago, just after the fall of Dunkirk, the one arm of- the British service that stood between us and invasion was the British navy. Yet we had never contributed a single dollar toward its upkeep or support in all those years. I invite the minister, therefore, to give us some information about these capital expenditures, and I should like him to defend Deep Brook. Why for a temporary installation it was necessary to spend $13,000,000 at Deep Brook-

1311588,ca.proc.d.1943-06-09.23.72,1943-06-09,29020af7-698a-475d-8d4d-dd9f2528d390,ca.m.3136,Mr. HAZEN:,,EDITION,,,I was surprised to hear the minister say that the contract price of Deep Brook was $8,000,000. I should like him to tell us how much of this item 4, $16,490,051.37, was spent on Deep Brook. The minister did not tell us last May when the training centre was to be established there, although in all probability plans had been decided on at that time. We were not told that the work was to be done without calling for tenders. I have some other questions I wish to ask the minister. We were not told that work was to be done without tenders, and we did not know why the undertaking was kept secret until it got under way. We did not know that this training school would cost, not $8,000,000 as the minister has said, but upwards of $12,000,000, or that the contract had been made on a cost plus a fixed fee basis, until a return was tabled in the house on March 30 of this year to a question asked by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black). According to the return, the estimated cost of the completed project is: Land, $55,200; buildings, $7,775,000; gradings and roadways,
' $227,000; drainage and water supply, $295,000; electric services, $248,000; wharves, $455,000; furniture and equipment, $733,000; other expenditures, $1,294,766, or a total of $11,082,966.

It seems to me that an expenditure of upwards of $12,000,000 to establish a naval training centre in the fourth year of the war calls for some explanation, and in my opinion it is open to criticism. Our present naval strength is between 55,000 and 60,000. Many of these men have completed training. The minister has told us that 20,000 are at sea; I have asked for figures showing how [Mr. R. B. Hanson.)

many are on land who have completed training; and the remaining number are now being trained at training centres that have been established at great cost in various parts of Canada. They are being trained, as the minister told us, at 18 R.C.N.V.R. divisions, sixteen or seventeen naval bases and training schools, at technical schools and universities and on ships. Why at this late date of the war, when the present naval strength is between 55,000 and 60,000, it is necessary to expend such an enormous sum of money for another training centre is a question which I think the minister should answer. Does the minister expect that this war will last forever? Does he count on an inexhaustible supply of man-power? Will he tell us what the size of the Canadian navy is to be when at full strength? Is there any over-all plan?

We know that Canada has plans to maintain an army overseas, an army consisting of two corps. Has any plan been made by the government to determine what the size of the Canadian navy is to be? It seems to me that at this stage of the war there should be some over-all plan. The government should know what its objectives are and exactly what it plans to do. When the Deep Brook training centre is completed, and I should like to know when it is expected that it will be completed, will any of the present training centres be closed? Is it the intention of the government to train both men and officers at Deep Brook? What is the nature of the training they are to receive there, and how long will the course or courses of training last which they are to receive?

The minister told us the other day that it requires six months' training for a man to qualify for the lowest rating. The return to which I have just referred, brought down for the bon. member for Cumberland, states that wheq, the work is completed, it is planned to have 6,000 men under training at one time and 2,178 of an operating staff. In other words, it will take 2-75 persons for every six persons being trained. The camp that was established at Debert in Nova Scotia cost about $5,000,000, and the Minister of National Defence told us the other day that it has accommodation or training capacity for 13,000 men. Here we are spending at least $12,000,000; it will probably be a great deal more than that before we are through, and we shall -have training capacity for only 6,000. At this late stage of the war when many thousands of men have been trained for the navy, when training centres have been established all over the country at a cost of millions of dollars, this expenditure is open to some criticism, and it is the duty of the min-
War Appropriation-Naval Services

ister to tell us why it had to be undertaken. Twelve million dollars is a tremendous sum of money, and to spend that money on a temporary building which will be torn down after the war, when there are training centres established all over the country, and to have it established at this late stage, is, I repeat, open to criticism. It is something that the minister will have to explain.

I simply placed on Hansard last night a series of quotations from speeches made by the hon. member for Broadview, dating back to 1926. Those were references to the Canadian navy. They were made one after the other-1926, 1928, 1940, 1942 and 1943. And I ended up by saying I had to have regard to the nature of those references rather than to the protestations whch the hon, member might have made last night.

This afternoon the hon. member rose in his place in the house, and spoke of personalities, asking why he should be singled out for attack, and stating again that he has been attacked. But nothing of the kind was done. If an hon. member in the house cannot quote the record of another hon. member on a certain point-in this instance the naval policy of Canada, and the quality of the Canadian navy-then we are coming to a curious state of affairs. And it is absurd for the hon. member for Broadview to attempt for one minute to shift the whole burden of proof, by saying that I

Not another bit of land was owned by the department, which was operating in rented buildings. We have had a great deal of difficulty in trying to get matters straightened out in Saint John, but I believe within a short time they will be straightened out. In Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, and everywhere else the navy was operating in that way; it did not own a single foot of land or a single building. I will say this, that the training facilities in this country are not at all sufficient for the training of our men. Furthermore, even though some men are trained at sea, a great many of them are being brought back for advanced courses. The question was made an order for return; it asked the cost of the property and the cost of the repairs, but the reply was, ""No information."" Then they went.
Questions

*over to Queen's Park crescent and took Sir Joseph Flavelle's house. My point is that there should be some coordination between the three departments on heavy repairs and maintenance, so as not to have this duplication and waste in the city of Toronto; and further that they should begin to look after the housing of our soldiers' families instead of putting people in mansions like those. There may be some explanation, but if there is the minister has never given it to me, and I think I am entitled to it.
